newsitem.title: FRANCE: No-sweat pantyhose make news at Paris undies show.
newsitem.headline: No-sweat pantyhose make news at Paris undies show.

text.p: Scented panty hose, bras that flatten a bustline and fabrics that fight bacteria and funnel away perspiration were among the new gimmicks on display at the International Lingerie Tradeshow on Monday.

Comfort and hygiene are new buzz words in the industry as lingerie makers respond to an increasing demand for bras, panties and stockings that flatten paunches and push up breasts without the torturous bindings of the Wonderbra.
"There's definitely a return to nature and well-being. In other words, lingerie that provides support but feels good," said Karine Attali of French hosiery firm Dim.

For the health-conscious, German chemicals firm Bayer has conceived "Stay Young Fabric", a honeycombed weave of spandex and nylon that massages the skin. It is said to help blood circulation and avoid redness, swelling and varicose veins.

Stay Young Fabric has been developed in conjunction with Keiko Ono, a New York-based Japanese entrepreneur who has just designed her first line of tank tops, bodysuits, leggings and brassieres using it.

"It's based on the physiological principle of diffuse, evenly displaced pressure on the skin. It's akin to a post-operative garment -- when you can't move, it keeps blood circulating freely through the body," said Richard Michael Wirin, vice-president of sales for Keiko Ono. "It's good for nurses, people who sit at computers all day."

Dim's latest product is a scented, anti-bacterial panty hose called "Souffle d'Air" (Breath of Air). Its airy weave of fine lycra allows the skin to breath, reducing perspiration, while its perfume veils unpleasant perspiration odours.
"The perfume holds for up to ten washings. And the stockings don't stick, which makes them cool in the summer," said Attali.

Italian textile firm Jersey Lomellina presented Coolmax, a fabric advertised as having "the property of keeping cool in the summer and stocking heat in the winter". Lingerie manufacturer Pascale Madonna is using it for her teddies, briefs and shorts.

For the full-figured woman, Colombian firm Leonisa has the "Fashion Control" bra which reduces a woman's bustline by two inches (five cm) thanks to a strip of power-net stretched diagonally across its synthetic lace cups.
"It minimises in a beautiful way, not like the big bras," said Leonisa spokeswoman Anna Urea.

Other novelties include seamless padded bras by French manufacturer Huit, Dim's "Hip confort" pantyhose with tough lycra panels that pull in flabby bellies and girdle the buttocks, and Dupont Nemours' Tactel Aquator, a synthetic that helps funnel away perspiration and is widely used for sportswear and bathing suits.
But in fashion, trends change before you can sneeze. A year from now, lingerie styles are expected to perform an about-face back towards the stays and bindings of corseting.
